gaps.title: Every staff account has MFA enrolled or is forced to enrol
gaps.message: 2 account(s) without MFA: kari.admin, ola.tech; new accounts are not required to enrol a second factor
gaps.action: Turn on two-factor login for every account
gaps.why: Staff accounts reach customer systems; a stolen password alone must not be enough.

gaps.should: Every account uses two-factor login, and new accounts must set it up.

gaps.title: Plain HTTP redirects to HTTPS and HSTS is set
gaps.message: HTTP does not redirect to HTTPS; no Strict-Transport-Security header
gaps.action: Send all website traffic over HTTPS
gaps.why: Without a redirect and HSTS, users can be kept on unencrypted HTTP.
gaps.found: Visitors who type http:// stay on the unencrypted site; browsers are not told to always use the encrypted site.
gaps.should: Visitors on http:// are sent to https://, and browsers are told to always use it.

narrative.executive_summary: The scan found gaps across every area it tested: all 17 checks failed, 21 requirements were not satisfied and 64 could not be assessed by this scan. The most serious gap is that the admin console accepts the default admin/admin login, which could give anyone full control. Other urgent gaps: the newest backups are 559 and 481 days old, two staff accounts lack multi-factor authentication, SSH allows password and direct root login, the web server still accepts outdated TLS versions, and running software contains fixable critical vulnerabilities.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require access control policies and require that login credentials are changed initially. The scan logged into the admin console with the username admin and password admin and was let in. Default credentials are widely known, so anyone who can reach the console could take full administrative control of the system.
remediation: Change the admin console password immediately to a unique, strong secret.
Ensure the default admin/admin combination is rejected, then re-run the check to confirm the login is refused.
Review console activity for signs that the default login was already misused.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require backup management and that backup copies of data are maintained. Each backup system holds a single snapshot: the newest borg backup is 559 days old and the newest restic backup is 481 days old, far beyond the maximum age the profile allows. If data were lost now, most recent work could not be restored.
remediation: Find out why scheduled backups for borg and restic stopped running and fix the cause.
Restore a regular backup schedule so the newest snapshot always stays within the profile's maximum age.
Set up an alert when backups stop, and re-run the check to confirm fresh snapshots exist.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules call for multi-factor authentication, especially for privileged and administration accounts. The accounts kari.admin and ola.tech have no second factor, and new accounts are not required to enrol one. A single stolen password would be enough to access these accounts, one of which appears to be an administrator.
remediation: Enrol a second factor for kari.admin and ola.tech.
Turn on the identity provider setting that forces new users to enrol multi-factor authentication.
Re-run the check to confirm no accounts remain without multi-factor authentication.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require that the strength of authentication matches the importance of what is being accessed. The SSH server, used for remote administration, accepts plain passwords alongside keys. Passwords can be guessed or stolen, which weakens protection of a sensitive entry point.
remediation: Configure the SSH server to stop offering password, keyboard-interactive and none authentication, keeping only public key login.
Make sure all administrators have working keys before the change.
Re-run the check to confirm password authentication is no longer offered.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require administration privileges to be individualised and restricted. SSH currently allows direct login as root (PermitRootLogin is 'yes'). This means attackers can target the most powerful account directly, and actions cannot be traced to an individual person.
remediation: Set PermitRootLogin to 'no' in the SSH server configuration.
Have administrators log in with personal accounts and raise privileges only when needed.
Re-run the check to confirm root login is disabled.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require policies on the use of cryptography. The server still accepts the outdated TLSv1 and TLSv1.1 versions in addition to TLSv1.2. Older versions have known weaknesses, so connections could be downgraded and traffic exposed.
remediation: Configure the server to refuse TLSv1 and TLSv1.1, keeping TLSv1.2 as the minimum.
Re-run the check to confirm only permitted versions are accepted.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require vulnerability handling, addressing critical vulnerabilities without undue delay, and applying security patches within a reasonable time. Of 8 running images scanned, several contain critical vulnerabilities for which fixes exist: nginx:1.20 (17), quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.3 (5), elasticsearch:8.19.10 (3), nis2lab-backup (3) and grafana/loki:3.5.1 (2). No risks have been formally accepted, and nginx:1.20 runs on an operating system that is no longer supported. Known, fixable flaws are a common route for attackers.
remediation: Update each listed image to a release that contains the available fixes and redeploy.
Replace nginx:1.20 with an image whose operating system is still supported.
Where a fix cannot be applied yet, record a formal risk acceptance.
Re-run the scan to confirm no fixable critical vulnerabilities remain.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require a complete, accurate and up-to-date asset inventory. Five running services are missing from it: backup, backup-borg, legacy-web, logs and search. Services that are not inventoried tend to be forgotten, left unpatched and unmonitored.
remediation: Add backup, backup-borg, legacy-web, logs and search to the asset inventory with an owner, or shut down any that are no longer needed.
Re-run the check to confirm no undeclared services remain.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require appropriate access controls on backup copies. The borg backup repository is not encrypted. Anyone who obtains a copy of the backups could read all the data in them.
remediation: Create an encrypted borg repository and move backups into it.
Store the encryption key securely and separately from the backups.
Re-run the check to confirm no unencrypted backup sets remain.

gaps.why_it_matters: The law requires staged reporting of significant incidents to the CSIRT, starting with an early warning within 24 hours. The incident response plan (incident-response.md) does not mention the 24h early warning, the 72h incident notification, the one-month final report or the CSIRT contact. During an incident staff may miss mandatory reporting steps.
remediation: Add the 24h early warning, 72h incident notification and one-month final report stages to incident-response.md.
Add the CSIRT contact details to the plan.
Re-run the check to confirm all stages are mentioned.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require blocking users after a predefined number of unsuccessful log-in attempts. Account lockout is disabled, so attackers can try unlimited passwords against any account.
remediation: Enable account lockout in the identity provider and set a maximum number of failed attempts.
Re-run the check to confirm lockout is enabled.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require authentication strength that fits the asset being accessed. There is no password policy and no minimum length, while the profile expects a minimum length of at least 12. Very short passwords are easy to guess.
remediation: Create a password policy in the identity provider with a minimum length of at least 12.
Re-run the check to confirm the policy is enforced.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require incident handling and keeping logs for a predefined period. Both elasticsearch (ILM policy logs-7d) and loki (retention_period 1w) delete logs after 7 days, while the profile expects at least 90 days. Incidents are often found late, and the evidence needed to investigate would already be gone.
remediation: Change the elasticsearch ILM policy so logs are kept at least 90 days.
Change the loki retention_period setting so logs are kept at least 90 days.
Re-run the check to confirm the new retention on both systems.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require policies on the use of cryptography. The server's certificate expired on 2025-01-01. Users see security warnings and learn to ignore them, and encrypted connections can no longer be properly trusted.
remediation: Replace the expired certificate with a valid one.
Set up automatic renewal or expiry alerts so the certificate is renewed well before it expires.
Re-run the check to confirm the certificate is valid.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require policies on the use of encryption. The website answers over plain, unencrypted HTTP without redirecting to HTTPS, and sends no Strict-Transport-Security header. Visitors may use an unencrypted connection that can be read or altered.
remediation: Configure the web server to redirect all plain HTTP requests to HTTPS.
Add the Strict-Transport-Security header to HTTPS responses.
Re-run the check to confirm both settings.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require incident handling. The incident response plan was last reviewed on 2023-02-14, 1320 days ago, while the profile expects a review at least every 365 days. An outdated plan may list wrong contacts, systems or steps.
remediation: Review and update incident-response.md and record the new review date.
Schedule reviews so the plan is never older than 365 days.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require access control policies. SSH allows 10 authentication attempts per connection, while the profile expects at most 4. More attempts per connection make password-guessing easier.
remediation: Set MaxAuthTries to 4 or lower in the SSH server configuration.
Re-run the check to confirm the new value.
